answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — actually John Heider
answer.authorDates: 1936–2010 · American clinical psychologist & Human Potential Movement teacher
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is John Heider’s, from The Tao of Leadership: Lao Tzu’s Tao Te Ching Adapted for a New Age (Humanics New Age, 1985) — a book whose own subtitle calls it an adaptation, not a translation. Taoism author Stefan Stenudd traces this line and its companion sentence to page 43 of Heider’s book ↗, very loosely spun from the opening lines of Tao Te Ching chapter 22. Standard translations of that chapter say nothing resembling it.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

None — Heider’s own free adaptation, not a rendering of the Chinese; his section 22 answers to Tao Te Ching chapter 22

source.excerpt:
When I let go of what I am, I become what I might be. When I let go of what I have, I receive what I need.

By yielding, I endure.

When I give of myself, I become more.
trail: Tao Te Ching chapter 22 does not contain this thought. The public-domain James Legge translation at Project Gutenberg ↗ opens the chapter “The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new” — about actions and states, not about becoming a different self.

Stefan Stenudd, who has published his own Tao Te Ching translation and commentary, devotes a page to this exact line ↗: he states plainly that it is not from the Tao Te Ching, names John Heider’s The Tao of Leadership (1985) as the source of both sentences, and cites page 43.
The wording is confirmable in the book itself: “Principles of Leadership: Excerpts from The Tao of Leadership” ↗ reproduces the passage verbatim, followed by “By yielding, I endure.”
The line is absent from the curated attribution record: Wikiquote’s Laozi page ↗ lists this sentence neither among his sourced quotations nor among the items it flags as misattributed.
source.excerptNote: These are Heider’s own sentences, verified verbatim in a circulated PDF of excerpts from the book ↗. A blog transcript of the passage places it under the heading “The paradox of letting go” ↗.

source.rightsNote: The idea reaches back to a text long in the public domain, but this wording does not. It was first published in 1985 by Humanics New Age ↗ as John Heider’s original composition, so it is a modern, in-copyright text and is quoted here only in brief. Public-domain translations of Tao Te Ching chapter 22, such as James Legge’s, are freely reusable — but they do not contain this sentence.

author.name: John Heider
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: John Heider — the psychologist behind the “Lao Tzu” line
author.metaLine: 1936–2010 · American clinical psychologist & Human Potential Movement teacher
author.bio: John Frederick Heider was born in Northampton, Massachusetts, on 7 November 1936, graduated from Harvard College in 1960 and took a Ph.D. in clinical psychology from Duke University in 1968. He joined the Esalen Institute as a resident fellow in September 1967 and stayed until 1971 as an encounter-group leader, later founding the Human Potential School of Mendocino; Esalen co-founder Dick Price encouraged the book and helped him find a publisher. The Tao of Leadership (1985) recast the Tao Te Ching as advice for people who run groups — and, ironically, its most-shared sentences now circulate under Lao Tzu’s name rather than his. He died at his home in Lawrence, Kansas, on 26 May 2010.

misattribution.heading: How it became a Lao Tzu quote
misattribution.intro: Heider’s book puts “Lao Tzu’s Tao Te Ching” on the cover and his own prose inside. Once the sentences were lifted off the page, the cover won: quote sites credit the ancient sage, or the ancient book, and drop the modern author entirely.

items.tag: Not in the Tao Te Ching
items.why: Stefan Stenudd’s Fake Lao Tzu Quotes ↗ states outright that this is not a quote from the Tao Te Ching, and argues the sentiment cuts against Lao Tzu, for whom “what I might be” would be precisely the illusion to drop. Goodreads nonetheless carries it under Lao Tzu’s name ↗, unsourced.

The two-sentence version circulates with the book as the “author”: Goodreads files “When I let go of what I am… When I let go of what I have, I receive what I need” under ‘Tao Te Ching’ ↗, with no chapter, edition or translator, and notes that community-added quotes are not verified.

items.scope: The chapter it is actually spun from
items.why: Heider’s section 22 answers to chapter 22, but that chapter is about yielding and wear, not self-reinvention: Legge’s public-domain translation opens “The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Taoism-flavoured; the sentence is not Taoist scripture. It was written in English by an American psychologist and first published in 1985 ↗.

context.heading: Adaptation, not translation
lead: The Tao of Leadership never pretended to be a translation. Its subtitle — “Lao Tzu’s Tao Te Ching Adapted for a New Age” — announces the licence Heider took, and he took a lot of it. The book renders the classic as a manual for running groups: short sections pairing a Taoist paradox with the practical business of facilitating people, drawn from the encounter-group work he had done at Esalen.

That framing is exactly what makes the book a misattribution engine. A reader who copies a sentence out of it keeps the aphorism and the cover’s promise of ancient authority, and loses the one fact that matters — that the English is Heider’s. Stenudd, who has translated and commented on the Tao Te Ching himself, calls the connection to chapter 22 so loose that it is hard to see how Heider got there from the Chinese.
detailsBody: James Legge’s public-domain translation begins: “The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. He whose (desires) are few gets them; he whose (desires) are many goes astray.” The chapter’s subject is the advantage of yielding and of not asserting oneself — it closes on the sage who does not strive, and with whom therefore no one in the world is able to strive.

Stenudd sets his own rendering of the opening (“Hulk to be whole. Bend to be straight. Empty to be filled. Wear down to be renewed…”) beside D. C. Lau’s to make the point that the chapter concerns actions and conditions, not remaking one’s identity into a better version.
context.pull: The cover said Lao Tzu. The sentences were Heider’s.
